extracted.intended_audience: political thinkers, lawmakers, and informed citizens debating constitutional change (late-18th-century British context)
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing when and how constitutions should be preserved, reformed, or overthrown; and what composition and principles should govern representative bodies. Grounded in Burkean conservative argument about inheritance, precedent, and the dangers of radical innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary inspection and impeachment as primary security
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliamentary oversight and the power of impeachment (as embodied in the Declaration of Right and statutes) provide better security for constitutional liberty than resorting to the removal/cashiering of governors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author contrasts constant parliamentary inspection and practical impeachment with the 'reservation of a right... so difficult in the practice, so uncertain in the issue' as means of securing rights and checking administration. Prefer institutional, legal remedies over extra-constitutional forcible removal.

rubrics_metrics.name: The king is sovereign in law, not a removable servant
rubrics_metrics.description: Although a king's power exists for public advantage, under the British Constitution he is not a servant who obeys another or is removable at pleasure; the law styles him 'our sovereign lord the king'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conceive of the monarch as a servant bound to obey private will; obedience is to law embodied in the crown. Language and practices that treat the king as a servant are inappropriate and ineffectual as constitutional devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: No constitutional provision to make the sovereign responsible like an ordinary servant
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution makes no provision for submitting the king to responsibility analogous to that of a servant (e.g., a Justicia of Aragon or a legally appointed court to try the monarch).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments or claims that 'a king... is... responsible to [the people]' contradict positive statute law and the structure of the British Constitution; such claims misunderstand constitutional form and precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cashiering (dethroning) a king is effectively an act of war, not a legal remedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Removing a monarch by force almost always becomes a case of war; 'laws are commanded to hold their tongues amongst arms,' and tribunals fall with the peace they cannot uphold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the practical consequences: overthrowing a sovereign leads to extra-legal, violent contest, collapse of legal institutions, and civil disorder. Treat questions of dethronement as extraordinary matters of state rather than matters of ordinary legal right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revolution must be the last resource and judged by gravity and probable consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: A revolution is 'the very last resource of the thinking and the good.' Its justification is not a question of positive rights but of necessity, dispositions, means, and probable consequences; the wise judge by the gravity of the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only when government is truly abused and deranged, and future prospects are as bad as past experience, is revolution defensible. The decision rests on sober prudential judgment, not abstract speculation or common agitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to 'frame a government for ourselves' lacks support from the Revolution's precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: The Revolution of 1688 aimed to preserve 'ancient indisputable laws and liberties' and the ancient constitution; it did not establish a general right to fabricate a new government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating claims to found a new government, look to historical precedent, parliamentary acts, and recorded statutes rather than rhetorical or pulpit proclamations. Constitutional change should be restorative/ preservative, not radical reinvention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reforms should proceed by reference to antiquity, analogical precedent, authority, and example
rubrics_metrics.description: All past reformations have been conducted 'upon the principle of reference to antiquity' and should be formed upon 'analogical precedent, authority, and example' rather than novel invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policymaking and constitutional reform should favor continuity with inherited practices and precedents; novelty is suspect and likely to produce instability. Use recorded examples and analogies to guide reform rather than abstract theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberties are an inherited patrimony; prefer positive recorded titles over speculative rights
rubrics_metrics.description: The law and historic documents (e.g., Magna Charta, Petition of Right, Declaration of Right) present liberties as an 'entailed inheritance'—a patrimony derived from forefathers—rather than vague 'rights of men'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims based on hereditary, recorded rights (titles, charters, statutes) are more secure and appropriate bases for liberty than speculative, abstract formulations of universal rights which risk scramble and instability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of inheritance secures conservation and transmission while allowing improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Treating government and liberties as inherited furnishes 'a sure principle of conservation, and a sure principle of transmission'—it secures gains while leaving acquisition free and allows improvement without radical novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor institutional continuity as a means to preserve accumulated advantages and restrain capricious innovation; see constitutional inheritance as analogous to property that is to be transmitted and conserved.

rubrics_metrics.name: A mixed constitution with opposing interests produces salutary checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Variety of parts, opposition of interests, and conflicting powers in an ancient constitution 'interpose a salutary check to all precipitate resolutions' and render deliberation necessary, producing moderation and compromise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design or preserve institutional pluralism and checks (different estates, interests) to prevent arbitrary power and rash reform; diversity of representation is a positive safeguard for liberty and stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative assemblies should be respectably composed (property, education, cultivated habits)
rubrics_metrics.description: To secure sobriety and moderation, assemblies should be composed 'in point of condition in life, of permanent property, of education, and of such habits as enlarge and liberalize the understanding.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eligibility and composition criteria for representatives should favor individuals with stable property interests, education, and character that promote deliberation and temperance. Avoid making sudden elevational experiments in composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assemblies dominated by lawyers and petty litigators risk a litigious, self-interested constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: When the bar's inferior, mechanical members predominate, the assembly tends toward a 'litigious constitution' and self-interested projects opening lucrative opportunities for those skilled in litigation and administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware overrepresentation of legal practitioners of the lower sort and other professional classes whose habitual concerns (petty litigation, procedural advantage) may bias institutional outcomes away from property stability and public good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Followers in assemblies must be qualified judges, otherwise they will be led blindly
rubrics_metrics.description: For leaders not to lead blindly, 'the followers must be qualified, if not for actors, at least for judges; they must also be judges of natural weight and authority.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that the electorate and represented body possess sufficient judgment, authority, and social weight to critically evaluate proposals and leaders; otherwise leadership will adapt proposals to the ignorance or passions of followers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Radical contempt for predecessors and romantic novelty produces social and moral ruin
rubrics_metrics.description: Despising predecessors and embracing extravagant speculations (ascribed to French leaders) produced 'poverty by crime,' insolent irreligion, corruption of manners, subversion of tribunals, commerce decline, and national ruin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate political innovations for their moral, economic, and institutional consequences. Romantic novelty and contempt for received institutions can produce widespread social, moral, and material calamity; prudence and respect for past practices are protective.
